title: Credentials from Password Stores
summary: Credentials from Password Stores is the parent behaviour of taking secrets from the places designed to hold them rather than from memory, network traffic or plain files. The locations differ by platform and product: browser password databases, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and Credential Locker, Linux keyring services, application configuration vaults and cloud secret managers. Because each store uses its own protection, the technique varies from decrypting a local database with a key that is itself recoverable, to convincing a broker process to release a secret on behalf of the calling user, to abusing an over-permissioned service account or automation token against a cloud vault. The common marker is not a specific command but a sequence: enumeration of the store, access through a client library or administration interface, and then authentication elsewhere with the recovered secret. Baselines of which processes normally open these stores are the strongest defence.

beginner.definition: Password stores are the built-in places where a computer keeps saved logins, such as a browser or an operating system keyring. This technique is when an attacker takes the saved passwords out of one of those stores. They do not break the encryption so much as open the store the way the owner would.
beginner.whyItMatters: Saved passwords are convenient, so people use them for many accounts. If one store is opened, the attacker gets many logins at once. They can then move between systems and services as the victim. This makes a single successful theft far more damaging.
howItWorks: Programs such as browsers and system keyrings save your passwords and tokens for you.
Each store protects its data with a key derived from your own login.
An attacker on the machine takes the store files and the related key material.
They copy the store, or ask its helper service to unlock it for them.
They now hold usernames, passwords, access tokens, private certificates and secure notes.
They reuse those stolen credentials on other hosts and inside cloud services.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where everyone keeps spare keys in a locked kitchen drawer. The drawer is strong, but each person unlocks it every morning for their own key. A visitor who learns the drawer routine can open it once and copy every spare key in the flat. A password store is that drawer, and one open moment releases all the keys.
takeaways: Password stores are a single point of loss, so protect the accounts around them.
Know which programs legitimately read each store so unusual readers stand out.
Rotate any credential that was ever shared in a message or ticket.

objectives: List the common password storage locations on Windows, macOS, Linux and in cloud services.
Explain the different ways a store can be opened or decrypted by an attacker.
Describe the telemetry that shows which process accessed a credential store.
Explain how stolen saved credentials support lateral movement.
Recommend monitoring and hardening practices for credential stores.
